relations.evidence: When a transaction executes a query statement, the transaction enters query mode, which means that the query is executed with the user's query permissions. Any key-value operations which are executed by the transaction _after_ the query statement are _also_ executed with the user's query permissions. These may or may not be different to the user's data permissions; if they are different, you may get unexpected results.

notable_absence.finding: This is the wave's priority target and the page delivers nothing on it. Across the full page there is not one Couchbase Server version number, not one 'since', 'as of', 'deprecated', 'removed in', 'Enterprise Edition' or 'Community Edition' string (verified by grep across all six pages of this batch). SQL++ transactions shipped in Server 7.0 and the whole Query Service transaction settings surface has changed across 7.x, yet the reference pages are entirely version-flat. The only version gate on the page is for a *client tool*: 'You must be using cbq shell version 2.0 or above.' Consequence for the ontology: on this tree, availableSince can only be populated from release notes or from the what's-new pages, never from the reference pages themselves - and any attempt to derive availableSince from the docs branch (release/8.0) would be a fabrication. That is why this record uses a separate minted documentedForVersion predicate for the branch fact.
notable_absence.secondary_finding: The Permissions section names role CATEGORIES ('the relevant _Administrative_ or _Data_ RBAC roles') and never a single named role or privilege, even though privilege:query-manage-index and role:full-administrator style ids exist in the registry. So requiresPrivilege cannot be populated for this statement family from this page either - the transaction family remains ungated at the individual-privilege level on Server exactly as the Capella records found it ungated at the credential-type level.

cross_component_finding: Two id-hygiene problems this record had to navigate, both for reconciliation to rule on. (1) The cbq shell already exists under two colliding ids in the extraction layer: n1ql:cbq (7 records, including all the Capella transaction twins) and tool:cbq-shell (4 records). I reused n1ql:cbq for continuity with my twins, but that leaves me minting tool:query-workbench and api:query-rest-api in different namespaces from the sibling surface they are listed alongside in one sentence of this page. The three query surfaces (Workbench / cbq / REST API) are one closed set on this page and should share a namespace. (2) sdk:transaction-query-mode is a promoted concept whose label says '(Java SDK transactions)' and whose id sits in the sdk: namespace, but the paragraph that defines it appears verbatim on this Server SQL++ reference page - it is a Query Service behaviour, not an SDK behaviour. The concept should be renamed and re-namespaced (transactions:query-mode or n1ql:query-mode) with sdk:transaction-query-mode kept as an alias; otherwise the graph asserts that a server-side permission-scope switch is a Java SDK feature.
cross_product_finding: This page is the strongest Server-vs-Capella divergence in the batch, on three separate axes. (1) ACCESS SURFACE, inverted: Server says 'To create a Couchbase transaction using SQL++, you can use any of the tools that you use to run a SQL++ query: the [Query Workbench](../../tools/query-workbench.md), the [cbq shell](../n1ql-intro/cbq.md), or the [Query REST API](../../n1ql-rest-query/index.md).' The Capella twin says only 'The [cbq shell](../n1ql-intro/cbq.md)' and adds an explicit exclusion note ('Couchbase Transactions are not supported via the Couchbase Capella Query tab or the Data API'). So Server supports three surfaces, Capella one. Crucially, the *stated cause* of the Capella exclusion ('The Query Service requires that the whole transaction must be executed by a single node') appears on the Server page too as the bare fact 'All statements within a transaction are sent to the same Query node' - the constraint is identical on both products; only the ability of the surface to honour it differs. The promoted incompatibleWithAccessSurface therefore needs a positive counterpart (supportedOnAccessSurface, minted here) or the graph reads as though transactions are surface-restricted everywhere. Note also that capella:query-tab and tool:query-workbench are both browser-based query editors in the same product family, yet one supports transactions with a dedicated 'Run as TX' button and the other cannot run them at all - a same-role, different-capability pair that must NOT be merged. (2) CONFIGURATION SCOPE: Server's settings table has 10 rows spanning request-level parameters, node-level settings and cluster-level settings (txtimeout/queryTxTimeout, atrcollection, cleanupclientattempts/queryCleanupClientAttempts, cleanuplostattempts/queryCleanupLostAttempts, cleanupwindow/queryCleanupWindow, numatrs/queryNumAtrs); Capella's has 7 rows and every single one is 'request-level parameter'. The entire node-level and cluster-level tier - i.e. everything about active-transaction-record placement, count, and lost/client cleanup - is invisible on Capella because it is operator-owned there. This is a deployment-keyed *scope* gate, not a feature gate: the feature exists on Capella, the knob does not. Predicates minted for it: hasSettingScope, hasScopeVariant. (3) PERMISSIONS MODEL, as the brief predicted: Server states RBAC role categories ('users must have the relevant _Administrative_ or _Data_ RBAC roles') where Capella states 'the relevant cluster access privileges'. Not merged. But the sharper divergence is that the Capella twin OMITS the entire Query Mode NOTE that this Server page carries - so the Capella docs never warn Capella users about the mid-transaction permission-scope switch at all, while the Server page and the Java SDK howto both do, in identical words. That looks like a Capella documentation gap rather than a behavioural difference.
